questions.question_text: A breakfast deal at a cafe is one of $8$ pastries with one of $5$ hot drinks. How many different breakfast deals are possible?

options.why: Added the two counts instead of multiplying, which counts the items on offer rather than the deals.
Multiplied the pastries by the number of stages ($8 \times 2$) instead of by the number of drinks.
Counted only the pastry choices and ignored the drink stage altogether.

questions.solution_text:
There are $8$ ways to choose the pastry and $5$ ways to choose the drink.
$8 \times 5$
$= 40$

questions.question_text: A burger shop combo is one burger, one side and one drink. There are $5$ burgers, $3$ sides and $4$ drinks. How many different combos are possible?

options.why: Added the three counts instead of multiplying them together.
Multiplied only the burgers and the sides, leaving out the drink stage.
Multiplied only the burgers and the drinks, leaving out the side stage.

questions.solution_text:
There are $5$ burgers, $3$ sides and $4$ drinks.
$5 \times 3 \times 4$
$= 60$

questions.question_text: A padlock uses a $4$-digit code. Each digit may be any of the digits $0$ to $9$, and digits may be repeated. How many different codes are possible?

options.why: Reduced the count at each position ($10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7$), assuming a digit could not be used twice.
Used only three positions, forgetting that the code has four digits.
Multiplied the $10$ digits by the $4$ positions instead of using $10$ once for each position.

questions.solution_text:
Each of the four positions has $10$ options, because digits may be repeated.
$10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10$
$= 10\,000$

questions.question_text: A membership card number is $2$ letters followed by $3$ digits, and letters and digits may be repeated. How many different card numbers are possible?

options.why: Reduced each count by one along the way ($26 \times 25 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8$), assuming no letter or digit could repeat.
Used only two digit positions instead of the three the card number has.
Multiplied the $26$ letters by the $2$ letter positions instead of using $26$ once for each position.

questions.solution_text:
Each letter position has $26$ options and each digit position has $10$.
$26 \times 26 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10$
$= 676 \times 1000$
$= 676\,000$

questions.question_text: A pizza deal is one pizza with one side. There are $5$ sides on the menu and $45$ different deals altogether. How many pizzas are on the menu?

options.why: Subtracted the number of sides from the total instead of dividing by it.
Multiplied the total by the number of sides instead of dividing, reversing the counting principle.
Added the number of sides to the total instead of dividing by it.

questions.solution_text:
Let $p$ be the number of pizzas.
$p \times 5 = 45$
$p = 45 \div 5$
$= 9$

questions.question_text: A cinema snack deal is one of $7$ snacks with one of $3$ drinks. The cinema then adds two more drinks to the menu. How many extra snack deals does this create?

options.why: Gave the new total number of deals instead of the increase in the number of deals.
Counted the extra deals from only one of the two new drinks.
Gave the number of new drinks, treating each new drink as exactly one new deal.

questions.solution_text:
Before the change:
$7 \times 3$
$= 21$
After the change there are $5$ drinks.
$7 \times 5$
$= 35$
$35 - 21$
$= 14$

questions.question_text: A car park code is one letter followed by two digits. The letter must be a consonant ($21$ of the $26$ letters) and the code must end in a $5$ or a $0$. Letters and digits may otherwise be repeated. How many codes are possible?

options.why: Applied the consonant restriction but let the last digit be any of the ten digits.
Applied the last-digit restriction but allowed all $26$ letters in the first position.
Ignored both restrictions and counted every letter and every digit as available.

questions.solution_text:
There are $21$ consonants, $10$ options for the middle digit, and $2$ options for the last digit.
$21 \times 10 \times 2$
$= 420$

questions.question_text: Lena has $6$ T-shirts and $5$ pairs of shorts, and wears one of each. She says she can make $11$ different outfits. Which statement best explains Lena's error?

options.text: Every T-shirt can be worn with every pair of shorts, so the counts multiply: $6 \times 5 = 30$ outfits.
Each pair of shorts is worn with one matching T-shirt, so there are $5$ outfits.
options.why: Pairs the items one to one instead of pairing every T-shirt with every pair of shorts.

options.text: The count is $6 \times 2 = 12$, multiplying the T-shirts by the number of stages.
options.why: Multiplies one stage's count by the number of stages rather than by the other stage's count.

options.text: Only the T-shirts change the outfit, so there are $6$ outfits.
options.why: Counts the options at one stage only and ignores the second stage entirely.

questions.solution_text:
Adding counts the number of items Lena owns, not the number of outfits.
Each of the $6$ T-shirts can be worn with any of the $5$ pairs of shorts.
$6 \times 5$
$= 30$

questions.question_text: A sandwich order is one bread, one filling and one sauce. A shop has $4$ breads, $5$ fillings and $3$ sauces. The owner can add exactly one new option, to just one of the three categories. Which choice creates the most new orders?

options.why: Assumes the category that already has the most options gives the biggest increase.
Ranks the categories by how many options they already hold instead of by the product of the other two.
Counts one extra order for each bread only, using $4$ instead of $4 \times 5$.

questions.solution_text:
$4 \times 5 \times 3$
$= 60$ orders at present.
With an extra bread:
$5 \times 5 \times 3$
$= 75$
With an extra filling:
$4 \times 6 \times 3$
$= 72$
With an extra sauce:
$4 \times 5 \times 4$
$= 80$
The largest total comes from a new sauce, creating $80 - 60 = 20$ new orders.
